body_markdown:
It is no cosmic coincidence that the first practical automobile and the first motion picture came into being within three years of each other. Both the 1885 Benz Patent-Motorwagen and Louis Le Prince’s 1888 3-second film of his family on vacation, known as *Roundhay Garden Scene* , were sibling offspring of the Industrial Revolution. The same gears and sprockets and springs and cams that drove a car and, increasingly, the world, could propel a reel of cellulose nitrate film through a mechanically operated shutter to produce sequential images. Which, when developed and fed back through a similarly mechanized projector, created humanity’s first moving pictures of itself.


Those earliest cinematographers were, not surprisingly, obsessed with motion—bustling street scenes, mounted horses in full stride, trains departing and arriving, and, inevitably, speeding cars. The first celluloid car chase is thought to be 1903’s *Runaway Match* , a 4.5-minute silent melodrama in which an apoplectic father pursues his eloping daughter and her lover in a pair of brass-era horseless carriages of the day. It has a number of hallmarks of much later films, including mounted cameras for car-to-car action, zooms, point-of-view shots, and establishing and pan shots. There’s even an explosion.


Since then, we’ve bought tickets and popcorn and sat down to watch jumping cars, swimming cars, flying cars, talking cars, killer cars, exploding cars, and cars that can travel through time. There have been cars that can drive themselves, cars that can fix themselves, cars that can shoot everything from grease to flames to missiles, and cars that can morph into robots. We’ve watched *Pink Cadillac, Cadillac Man, The Lincoln Lawyer, Corvette Summer, Car Wash, Duel, Dude, Where’s My Car?, The Car, Used Cars, Drive, Taxi Driver, Baby Driver, Driving Miss Daisy, Grand Prix, Gran Torino, Grand Theft Auto,* *Two-Lane Blacktop, The Road Warrior, The Cannonball Run, The Fast and the Furious,* and, of course, *Speed.*


Picture cars roll down the Queensboro Bridge during production of *The Great Gatsby* in New York City on July 15, 1973.


Fairchild Archives/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images


Cars could probably exist without movies, but it’s questionable whether movies could exist as a viable industry without cars. “Cars are symbolic to the audience, particularly an American audience where cars have long been a symbol of freedom and change,” Steve Morris told me. He’s a Los Angeles–based film director, instructor, and writer who co-hosts a movie-analysis podcast called *The CineFiles* , of which I happen to be a fan. “You go from Jack Kerouac’s *On the Road* to the Joads loading up the truck in *The Grapes of Wrath* to Marty McFly in the DeLorean, and in all of those, the vehicle is a symbol of the journey, of the change in life, of the transformation. That’s why cars have such a profound experience in the world of film, because we connect them emotionally to so much stuff in our lives.”


Making a movie takes writers, producers, and an army of production people. Plus, a troupe of actors and a director working together over months and sometimes years in a grueling multimillion-dollar enterprise that at times resembles a military campaign. Morris, who has also taught directing and is writing a book on the subject (the first chapter of which discourages people from entering the profession), says all of that effort is expended just to grab the audience’s attention for a short time and tell a story. With some movies costing more than a million dollars a minute, screen time is precious. Thus, as Morris often says on his podcast, everything you see on screen represents a choice.


Meaning that each frame of film—all 24 frames per second, or 130,000 frames in a 90-minute feature—has been painstakingly constructed and curated like a museum diorama to advance a story. If a tree is blocking part of a shot, it’s for a reason. If a shadow falls across part of an actor’s face, it’s for a reason. If the hero drives a souped-up Trans Am, it’s for a reason. In the 1996 comedy hit *Swingers* , when struggling actor Mike Peters, played by Jon Favreau, bashfully approaches an attractive woman at a Hollywood Hills party, she bluntly asks him, “What kind of a car do you drive?” It’s an existential question in film; what you drive is frequently who you are in a movie.


Lead actors Vince Vaughn and Jon Favreau in character in the cult-classic comedy *Swingers.*


Miramax


Annette O’Toole, Nick Nolte, and Eddie Murphy starring in *48 Hrs* .


Paramount/Getty Images


Nick Nolte in *48 Hrs* . clanks through San Francisco in a rusty, trash-strewn ’64 Caddy because he’s an old, broken-down cop whose life, like the car, is a disorganized mess. Kevin Bacon rocks a battered VW Beetle in *Footloose* because he’s poor but also an outsider in a rural American town where everyone else drives pickups. The director doesn’t even need to show the car for the car to be important to advancing the story. In *Swingers* , that 15-second exchange early in the film is packed with information: The question, “what kind of a car do you drive,” shows the audience how shallow and materialistic Hollywood can be, while the mumbled answer, a red Chevy Cavalier, indicates that Peters is dull and practical and not exactly up to L.A. spec, and he knows it.


> Cars have such a profound experience in film because we connect them emotionally to so much stuff in our lives.


“When humans meet other humans,” explains Morris, “they don’t get handed a résumé bio and important facts about that person. You assess a person based on their appearance, on their attitude, on their movement, on everything that they do.” Ditto the human audience meeting a new character in a movie. The car, particularly if it’s a good choice, “tells you way more emotionally about a character than a description, or words, or facts,” says Morris.


Actor Al Pacino sitting in a motor racing car, filming scenes for the movie *Bobby Deerfield* , Le Mans, France, circa 1977.


Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images


If what you drive in a movie is who you are, then what everyone else drives is typically where you are. In one single shot of a street, a director can evoke the era in which the film is set. If the cars have spoked wheels and bustleback trunks, it’s the 1930s. Art deco streamlining, the 1940s. Fins and chrome, the ’50s, and so on. And it’s not simply the time period being established with that one shot; it’s the clothes, the politics, the gender roles, the race relations, the music and popular culture, the rules of language—indeed, the whole immersive environment in which the ensuing story will play out. The cars on the street often go a long way toward prepping the audience for what is to come in the rest of the film. Over the past 125 years, cars have proven vital to cinematic storytelling even when the story isn’t about cars at all.


Sometimes the story is about cars—or, at least, it revolves around cars. Morris told me the only true movie about cars is *Cars* , the Pixar animated comedy from 2006. And, as he points out, that film isn’t really about cars, it’s about people played by anthropomorphized cars. The same goes for the jealous, vindictive lover played by a 1958 Plymouth Fury in *Christine* . Or the pitiless serial killer played by a George Barris–customized 1971 Lincoln in *The Car* . Or the lovable scamp played by Herbie the Volkswagen in the titular comedy franchise.


20 years on, Lightning McQueen is still a highly loved and recognizeable IP as the protagonist from the animated franchise *Cars* .


Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images


Though the cars in those movies are undeniably prominent characters in their stories, they tend not to be our favorite car movies. That’s because a sentient, self-driving car with the emotions of a human is unrealistic (and probably will continue to be for at least a few more years). In the car movies we love the most, the cars need the humans to perform, yet they are more than just props—they are characters themselves. The definition of a “character,” says Morris, isn’t limited to people or animals. It can be any entity that has a personality, has quirks, and to which the audience develops an emotional attachment. If a vehicle does all that, then “at that point, it has become a character,” he says.


In *Star Trek* , for example, “the Starship *Enterprise* is a character, and we know it’s a character because we’re emotionally moved in *Star Trek III* , where Kirk is supposed to blow up the love of his life.” In the *Mad Max* series, the black Interceptor has relatively little screen time, yet we are sad when it sacrifices itself to save Max. Who doesn’t cheer the Trans Am in *Smokey and the Bandit* as it jumps and careens to keep the caper rolling toward its impossible deadline? James Bond usually works alone—except for his faithful Aston Martin packing hidden machine guns and an ejector seat. The car is his partner.


Which is why celluloid cars are so frequently more than mere props. They can define the main characters, set the background for the story, and even become characters themselves. In other words, just like the cars in your garage, the ones that define you, that tell your backstory and have sparked an emotional connection. What kind of car do you drive? It’s as important a question in your own personal movie as it is on the silver screen.
